lesson.text: Quick memory: what are inputs and outputs? (Inputs take things in, like a touch screen; outputs give things out, like a speaker.) Today: technology everyone can use.
People use technology in different ways. Some can't see well or at all, and some can't hear. Some find reading hard, and some can't use their hands on a screen.
Captions show the words spoken in a video. They help deaf people, and anyone watching in a noisy place or learning a new language.
A screen reader reads the screen aloud for people who can't see it. Pictures need alt text, a short description, so the screen reader can say what they show.
Big text, zoom and high contrast (bright text on a dark screen) help people who see a little. Voice control and switches let people use a device without touching it.
Worked example: a game map shows safe paths in green and danger in red, and nothing else. About 1 in 12 boys can't easily tell red from green, so good designers add shapes or words too.
Louis Braille, who was blind, invented braille in the 1820s: raised dots read by touch. Today braille displays turn a screen's words into dots. This School reads every card aloud too.
Try it in the world: with a grown-up, turn on captions or read-aloud on a device at home. Who else would they help? Next, in grade 6: binary, the numbers computers use.

exercises.prompt: Match each feature to who it helps most.
exercises.hint: Captions are words to read; a screen reader speaks.
exercises.explain: Captions help people who can't hear well, screen readers people who can't see, voice control people who can't use their hands, and big text people who see a little.

exercises.hint: Have you ever watched a video somewhere noisy?
exercises.explain: False: captions also help in noisy places, in quiet places, and when learning a language.

exercises.hint: What does a screen reader need to say what a picture shows?
choices: a short description of a picture
exercises.explain: Alt text is a short description of a picture, which a screen reader reads aloud.

exercises.hint: Look at the words at the bottom of the video.
exercises.explain: The spoken words are shown under the video: captions.

exercises.hint: Look at the speaker next to the lines of text.
exercises.explain: The speaker shows the screen's words being read aloud.

exercises.prompt: A game map shows safe paths in green and danger in red only. How could it help colour-blind players?
exercises.hint: What could someone use if they can't tell the two colours apart?
choices: Add shapes or words as well as colours
exercises.explain: Shapes or words as well as colours mean nobody needs to tell red from green.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: does it help with seeing, or with hearing?
items: a doorbell that flashes a light
exercises.hint: Does it make something easier to see, or does it show a sound?
exercises.explain: Big text, screen readers and high contrast help with seeing. Captions and a flashing doorbell help with hearing.

exercises.prompt: Voice control lets someone use a device without touching it.
exercises.explain: True: you speak, and the device does what you say.

exercises.prompt: Which alt text is most helpful for a photo of a red boat on a lake?
exercises.hint: Which one tells someone who can't see it what is in the picture?
choices: A red boat on a calm blue lake
exercises.explain: A red boat on a calm blue lake says what the picture shows. The others tell a listener nothing.

exercises.prompt: Why is designing for everyone good for everyone?
exercises.hint: Who else used captions in a noisy place?
choices: Features like captions help lots of people
Only a few people use them
exercises.explain: Features made for some people, like captions, turn out to help lots of others too.

exercises.prompt: About 1 in 12 boys is colour-blind. In a school with 240 boys, about how many is that?
exercises.hint: Share the 240 boys into groups of 12.

exercises.prompt: Louis Braille invented a way to read by touch. What is braille made of?
exercises.hint: You read it with your fingertips.
exercises.explain: Braille is raised dots, felt with the fingertips.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: input (you give it to the device) or output (the device gives it to you)?
exercises.hint: Does it take something in, or give something out?
exercises.explain: Voice control and a switch are inputs. Captions, a screen reader and big text are outputs.

exercises.prompt: Louis Braille, who invented braille, was blind himself.
exercises.hint: Think of the card about braille.
exercises.explain: True: Louis Braille was blind from when he was 3, and he invented braille as a teenager.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem to a design that solves it.
items: a video, for a deaf viewer
a photo, for a blind reader
exercises.hint: Who cannot hear, see, tell colours apart, or read small print?
exercises.explain: Captions show a deaf viewer the words. Alt text lets a screen reader describe the photo. Shapes or words help players who cannot tell red from green. Zoom and big text help people who see a little.
